newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Asian economies cautiously welcome U.S. chip data.
newsitem.headline: Asian economies cautiously welcome U.S. chip data.

text.p: Asian economies that depend heavily on semiconductor exports saw a glimmer of hope in U.S. industry data indicating healthier sales, but analysts said on Wednesday it was too early to celebrate.
On Tuesday the U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association said its book-to-bill ratio, which measures new orders against shipments, rose to 0.90 in August from a revised 0.86 in July.
That means that for every $100 of semiconductors they shipped, suppliers received $90 in new orders.
South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and Singapore have invested heavily in the production of semiconductors and their economies have been hit by plunging international prices.
Analysts cautioned it was too early to draw optimistic conclusions from the August data, adding it would take months for Asian economies to feel any benefits.
"It is just one month's figure," said Yang Sy Jian, research director at RHB-Cathay Securities in Singapore. "We need at least the September figures to confirm the upward trend."

In South Korea, where semiconductors account for almost 20 percent of exports, there was a flurry of excitement on the local stock market as investors anticipated the news on Tuesday. Profit-taking eroded the gains on Wednesday.

"The marginal improvement in the book-to-bill ratio won't have a big impact on the industry here," said Philip Uhm, an electronics analyst at BZW Securities in Seoul. "The rise in the ratio stemmed more from a decrease in billings than a gain in new orders."
U.S. figures showed new orders rose 0.9 percent last month to $2.84 billion from $2.82 billion in July, while billings declined 3.2 percent to $3.15 billion against $3.26 billion.
International spot prices of 16 megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips fell to $12 a unit in August, from $50.10 a year ago.
Economists and analysts in Singapore said the latest data had done little to change their generally bearish view of the electronics sector in Asia over the next six months.
While they were heartened by the rise in the ratio they noted that new orders were still down 37.8 percent year-on-year in August.

Electronics and related products account for around half Singapore's industrial production and 60 percent of its non-oil exports. As a result, Singapore's economy tends to closely follow the performance of the U.S. electronics industry.
Liew Yin Sze, chief economist at brokerage J.M. Sassoon, said there were signs that inventory reductions in the electronics industry were already well under way.

"But even if the U.S. numbers start ticking up in September or October this year, it will still be March or April of next year before Asian economies feel the benefit," he said. "The book-to-bill ratio is essentially a six-month leading indicator."
Brokers in Taiwan said the August ratio, while improved, was below expectations.

"August and September should be a hot-sale season for the semiconductor industry, so the August ratio, though improved, was poorer than expected," said Ben Lee of Nomura Securities in Taipei. "I would say Taiwan's semiconductor industry has not fully bottomed out, but a gradual recovery is expected."
Brokers in Tokyo said the U.S. ratio was well within expectations.
"Rather than the book-to-bill ratio itself, the market focus is on the earning forecasts of semiconductor-related firms," one broker said.
According to the U.S. trade group, Japan's book-to-bill ratio exceeded 1.02 in July, the latest period available.
